title: SGA / LGA & Birth Injury
sources: Critical Vector — Neonatology Pocket Guide: SGA/IUGR & LGA; Birth Injury
ACOG/SMFM FGR guidance; standard neonatology teaching

changelog.change: Initial entry — SGA symmetric vs asymmetric, LGA/macrosomia, the scalp-haemorrhage distinction, and brachial plexus palsy patterns.

purpose: Recognise the growth-abnormal newborn (and anticipate the metabolic complications), and distinguish the benign scalp haemorrhages from a subgaleal bleed that can exsanguinate.

body.text: Birth weight < 10th percentile for gestational age. FGR implies a pathologic in-utero process; SGA alone with normal Dopplers and interval growth is often constitutionally small.

rows: Symmetric (early onset)
Weight, length, AND head circumference proportionally reduced
Early insult — chromosomal / genetic disorder, congenital (TORCH) infection
Asymmetric (late onset)
Weight affected more than length/HC (head relatively spared)
Late uteroplacental insufficiency

items: Complications: perinatal asphyxia, meconium aspiration, hypothermia, hypoglycaemia, hypocalcaemia, polycythaemia (→ hyperbilirubinaemia).
Management: early and frequent feeds, glucose monitoring, thermoregulation, check haematocrit.
Birth weight > 90th percentile for gestation, or ≥ 4000 g at term.
Most common cause: infant of a diabetic mother (maternal hyperglycaemia → fetal hyperinsulinaemia → growth acceleration). Also constitutional, post-term, Beckwith-Wiedemann.
Complications: shoulder dystocia, brachial plexus injury, clavicle fracture; hypoglycaemia (especially IDM); polycythaemia, hyperbilirubinaemia; respiratory distress.

rows: Caput succedaneum
Diffuse scalp oedema; CROSSES suture lines; may be ecchymotic
Present at birth; resolves in days
Cephalohaematoma
Subperiosteal; limited to ONE cranial bone; does NOT cross sutures
May enlarge over days; resolves over 2 weeks–3 months; associated linear skull fracture in a minority
Subgaleal haemorrhage
Beneath the galea; CAN cross sutures and spread broadly — large concealed blood loss
Potentially life-threatening; most associated with vacuum extraction. Serial head circumference + haematocrit + vitals
Subconjunctival / retinal haemorrhage
Common even after a normal delivery
Resolves in ~ 2 weeks; not pathologic in isolation

body.text: Subgaleal haemorrhage is the birth-related cranial injury that causes haemodynamic instability — a boggy, expanding scalp swelling that shifts with position, a rising head circumference, pallor, and tachycardia after a vacuum delivery. Monitor closely, transfuse, and correct coagulopathy. Do not lump it with caput/cephalohaematoma.

rows: Erb-Duchenne (C5–C6, upper trunk)
Most common. 'Waiter's tip' — arm adducted, internally rotated, forearm pronated. Absent biceps reflex, asymmetric Moro. Hand GRASP PRESERVED (favourable sign)
Klumpke (C8–T1, lower trunk)
Less common. Clawed, paralysed hand; absent grasp reflex. Ipsilateral Horner syndrome (ptosis, miosis) if T1 sympathetic fibres involved

body.text: Most recover substantially; upper-trunk (Erb) has a better prognosis than lower-trunk (Klumpke). Management: gentle range-of-motion exercises, monthly follow-up; surgical referral if no meaningful recovery by ~ 3 months. Always check for a co-existing clavicle or humerus fracture and for phrenic-nerve involvement (respiratory distress).

buildNote: Combines SGA/LGA and birth injury (linked by shoulder dystocia / macrosomia).
